subtitleEn: A day of rest not to be forgotten
heTitleNote: Shabbat day, at the second meal
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | A A | Dm Dm |
metaLine: 96 BPM · 4/4 · Shabbat lunch · five stanzas of four lines, every line in the poem ending on the same syllable, answered by a two-line refrain
intro: Judah Halevi wrote this, and the refrain is the reason to learn it: the dove found rest there, and there the exhausted will rest. The dove is Noah's, sent out over the water and coming back because there was nowhere to land — and the poem makes the Sabbath the place she was looking for. Every single line of the poem, refrain included, ends on the same syllable, which is a piece of technical showing-off you can hear without knowing any Hebrew at all.

stanzas.label: not to be forgotten

lines.en: A day of rest, not to be forgotten —
its memory is like a pleasing fragrance.
The dove found rest in it,
and there the weary of strength will rest.
The dove found rest in it, and there the weary of strength will rest.

stanzas.summary: {{1.1}} and {{1.2}} are the sacrificial phrase from Leviticus, a pleasing fragrance, applied here to a memory rather than to smoke. And every line ends in the same sound: {{0.3}}, {{1.2}}, {{2.3}}, {{3.3}}. That single rhyme runs through all twenty-five lines of the poem.

stanzas.label: carved on stone

lines.en: This day is honoured by the children of the faithful,
careful to keep it, parents and children;
it is engraved on two tablets of stone,
out of great vigour and mighty strength.
The dove found rest in it, and there the weary of strength will rest.

stanzas.summary: {{7.0}} means carved into stone, not written on it, and the poem is precise about the difference: the commandment is cut into the material rather than laid on top of it.

stanzas.label: we will do and we will hear

lines.en: And they all entered into the covenant together;
we will do and we will hear, they said as one,
and they opened their mouths and answered: the LORD is one.
Blessed is He who gives strength to the weary.
The dove found rest in it, and there the weary of strength will rest.

stanzas.summary: {{11.0}} and {{11.1}} are the two words Israel says at Sinai in Exodus 24 — we will do and we will hear, in that order, which has been the subject of commentary ever since. {{13.1}} through {{13.3}} is a line from the morning blessings, so the stanza runs from Sinai to this morning.

stanzas.label: remember and keep

lines.en: He spoke in His holiness on the mountain of myrrh:
the seventh day — remember it and keep it;
and all His commandments, to complete them together,
brace the loins and gather strength.
The dove found rest in it, and there the weary of strength will rest.

stanzas.summary: {{16.2}} and {{16.3}} are the two verbs of the two versions of the commandment, remember and keep, put in one line — the same move Menucha VeSimcha makes on Friday night. {{15.3}} is the mountain of myrrh from the Song of Songs, used here as a name for Sinai.

stanzas.label: the oath

lines.en: The people that wandered like a lost flock —
may He remember to keep His covenant and His oath to them,
so that no evil may befall them,
as You swore concerning the waters of Noah.
The dove found rest in it, and there the weary of strength will rest.

stanzas.summary: The last line names the dove's flood, which the refrain has been alluding to for five stanzas without saying so. {{23.4}} is Noah, and {{23.3}} his waters — the oath is Isaiah 54, where God swears never to flood the earth again. The poem has been building to this word since its first refrain.

chantTips: The refrain is eight words and returns five times. It is also the only part with a name in it, so it is the part people remember.
Every line of the whole poem ends on the same syllable. If you are singing by ear and a line does not land on it, you have gone wrong.
Around 96 BPM, steady. Slower than Yom Zeh Mechubad, which usually precedes it at the same table.
Sung at lunch. Some tables take it after the fish and before the meat, which is as good a reason as any.

about.body: Eleventh and twelfth century, Spain, and the poet whose name is attached to more Hebrew verse still sung today than almost anyone's. The Daat edition names him in a closing line, which is editorial matter rather than part of the song and was removed by the scaffold.

Genesis 8: the dove goes out from the ark, finds no resting place for the sole of her foot, and comes back. The poem takes the word for that resting place and makes the Sabbath into it, then waits until the last line of the last stanza to mention the flood at all.

A monorhyme of this length is a formal exercise inherited from Arabic poetry, and Halevi was working in a tradition where it was expected. The effect on a singer is practical rather than decorative: it makes the whole poem one continuous shape instead of five separate stanzas.
